lesson.title: The Accumulator Pattern: Building One Answer Across Many Iterations
lesson.summary: The accumulator pattern uses a variable initialized before a loop and updated on every pass to build up a single running result, such as a sum, product, or combined string, by the time the loop finishes.
lesson.body:
The accumulator pattern is one of the most useful loop patterns because so many real problems boil down to combining a whole collection of values into just one final answer: a total, an average, a longest string, a running count. The pattern has three consistent ingredients that always appear together. First, you initialize an accumulator variable before the loop begins, set to whatever starting value will not distort the final result at all, 0 for a sum, 1 for a product, an empty string for concatenation, an empty list for collecting items along the way. Second, inside the loop body, you update that exact same variable on every single pass, usually with augmented assignment. Third, once the loop finishes running entirely, the accumulator holds the finished result, ready to be used for whatever comes next.

Here is the pattern building a sum:
grades = [85, 92, 78, 90]
total = 0
for grade in grades:
    total += grade
average = total / len(grades)
print(average)
Trace the accumulator across every single pass. Before the loop begins, total is 0. grade is 85: total becomes 0 + 85 = 85. grade is 92: total becomes 85 + 92 = 177. grade is 78: total becomes 177 + 78 = 255. grade is 90: total becomes 255 + 90 = 345. The loop ends with total holding 345, the complete sum built up one grade at a time across four separate passes. After the loop, average is computed as 345 divided by len(grades), which is 4, giving 86.25, and that final value is what gets printed to the screen.

The starting value matters more than it might first seem. Starting a sum accumulator at 0 works because 0 is the identity value for addition, adding it to anything leaves that thing completely unchanged. A product accumulator, by contrast, must start at 1, not 0, because 1 is the identity value for multiplication instead; starting a product accumulator at 0 is a classic beginner bug, since multiplying anything by 0 collapses the entire running result down to 0 permanently, no matter what values come afterward in the loop.

This pattern is inseparable from augmented assignment: total += grade is shorthand for total = total + grade, and applying that exact operation to the same variable, once per pass, is precisely what turns an ordinary loop into a working accumulator. Without reusing the same variable consistently across every single iteration, there would be nothing actually accumulating at all, just a fresh value being calculated and immediately discarded each time through.

As the most common member of the loop patterns family, the accumulator pattern underlies far more than manual sums alone. Built-in functions like sum() are, conceptually, this exact pattern already written for you ahead of time, and the same three-step structure, initialize, update every pass, use the final result, reappears whenever you build a filtered list, join strings together, or track a running maximum value across an entire collection of data.
